text.en: On a hot day Meena noticed that the iron rails of a railway track have small gaps. "Metals expand," said her teacher.

Temperature describes how hot or cold a body is. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature. Add 273.15 to a Celsius reading to get kelvins. School calculations often round this to 273.
Most substances expand as temperature rises. We can measure changes in length, area and volume. For a liquid in an expanding container, the observed expansion is smaller than the real expansion by the increase in container volume.
For a fixed amount of gas, Boyle's law relates pressure and volume at constant temperature. Charles's law relates volume and absolute temperature at constant pressure. Avogadro's law relates volume to amount of gas at constant pressure and temperature. An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT, with R ≈ 8.31 J per mol per K.
Temperature is the degree of hotness of a body, and thermal energy flows from the hotter body to the colder.
Heat is energy transferred between bodies or regions because they have different temperatures.
For a Celsius reading, add about two hundred and seventy-three to get its value in kelvins. Bodies in thermal equilibrium have the same temperature.
Most substances expand as their temperature increases. We can describe the change in the length, surface area or volume.
Real gases tend to behave more like ideal gases at low pressure and sufficiently high temperature.

For a fixed amount of gas, Boyle's law keeps temperature constant, and Charles's law keeps pressure constant. Avogadro's law compares the volumes of different amounts of gas at the same temperature and pressure.
An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J per mol per K.
A mug and a large pot of water can have the same temperature. The pot holds more water, so it can contain more thermal energy even at that same temperature.
Put a warm object next to a cooler one. Energy transfers from the warmer object to the cooler one, reducing their temperature difference.
When objects in thermal contact reach the same temperature, that temperature difference is gone. There is no net flow of heat between them.

board.text: Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer

text.en: The same temperature can be reported with either scale. Zero degrees Celsius converts to two hundred and seventy-three point one five kelvins.

board.text: Use Celsius or kelvins for temperature

text.en: The two scales have equal-size intervals. Their starting points differ, so add the offset only to a temperature reading, not to a change.

board.text: A 10 °C rise is a 10 K rise

text.en: Joule is the SI unit of transferred energy. A calorie is another unit of energy and is about four point two joules.
A warmed metal strip usually lengthens. A sheet grows in two dimensions, and a solid block can increase in volume.

board.text: Expansion can affect length, area and volume

text.en: Compare two rods of the same material warmed by the same amount. The longer rod gains more length.

board.text: Linear expansion depends on starting length

text.en: Two rods of equal starting length can gain different lengths after the same temperature rise. Their expansion coefficients describe this difference.

board.text: Expansion also depends on the material

text.en: Expansion joints allow sections to lengthen on a warm day and shorten on a cold day. The gaps make room for these changes.
Imagine a flask that holds a liquid. When its temperature rises, the liquid and the flask can increase in volume.

board.text: A liquid and its container can both expand

text.en: The liquid level shows the extra volume relative to the expanded flask. Add the flask’s increase to that observed change to find the actual liquid expansion.

board.text: Real expansion = apparent expansion + container expansion

text.en: Pressure, volume, temperature and amount can all change. Each simple gas law holds selected quantities fixed so we can compare the other two.

board.text: Read a gas law’s fixed conditions

text.en: Take a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature. When its pressure doubles, its volume halves in the ideal model.
At two atmospheres and six litres, the product is twelve atmosphere-litres. At four atmospheres, three litres gives that same product.
Keep pressure and the amount of gas constant. Volume and kelvin temperature rise in the same ratio.
A gas occupying four litres at three hundred kelvins occupies six litres at four hundred and fifty kelvins when the pressure and amount stay fixed.

board.text: From 300 K to 450 K means a factor of 1.5

text.en: If the amount doubles in a flexible container and pressure and temperature stay fixed, the ideal-gas volume doubles.

board.text: Avogadro: add gas while pressure and temperature stay fixed

text.en: In P V equals n R T, n counts the amount of gas in moles. Temperature T is measured in kelvins.

board.text: A mole is a unit for the amount of substance

text.en: With R about eight point three one joules per mole per kelvin, use pressure in pascals and volume in cubic metres.
At fixed amount and temperature, the right side of P V equals n R T is constant. This gives Boyle’s relation between pressure and volume.

text.en: At high pressure, gas particles are much closer together. Their size and interactions matter more, so the ideal equation can be less accurate.
When pressure rises in a constant-temperature Boyle problem, the volume should fall. If your number shows the opposite, check which pressure belongs with which volume.

problem.en: In a model, a flask expands by 2 mL and the observed increase of liquid is 5 mL. How much did the liquid’s volume increase?

text.en: Add 2 mL to the observed increase of 5 mL.

why.en: The flask can hold 2 mL more before the level shows an increase.

text.en: The actual liquid expansion is 7 mL.

why.en: Apparent expansion was measured relative to the expanding flask.

problem.en: A fixed amount of gas occupies 4 L at 300 K. Its pressure stays the same and it warms to 450 K. Find the new volume.

text.en: Use V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.

why.en: Charles’s law uses the kelvin scale at fixed pressure and amount.
The absolute temperature and volume increase by the same factor.

problem.en: A gas at 300 K occupies 0.02493 m³ at pressure 100,000 Pa. Estimate the amount in moles using R = 8.31.

text.en: Rearrange PV = nRT to n = PV/(RT).

why.en: Use pressure in pascals, volume in cubic metres and kelvin temperature.
Both numerator and denominator evaluate to 2493 in compatible units.

points.en: Heat flows from hot to cold.
